# Edualist

> International school consulting and parent-student coaching for Turkish families relocating abroad, founded by Özlem Çimen in Dubai.

Edualist helps Turkish families navigate international school selection, curriculum evaluation, admissions processes, and student adaptation when moving abroad — especially to Dubai, UAE. Founded by Özlem Çimen, an education professional with 20+ years of experience and an expat mother who raised two children across five countries.

## About the Founder

Özlem Çimen is an international education consultant and parent-student coach based in Dubai, UAE.

- 20+ years as English teacher, department head, and school administrator at TED Istanbul College, ENKA Schools, and Istanbul International Community School (IICS)
- Expat mother: lived and schooled children in Singapore, Myanmar, France, Azerbaijan, and UAE
- MBA in International Marketing (USA)
- Certified in Child Protection, Differentiated Instruction (Harvard Graduate School of Education), and IB Curricula
- Expert in EAL (English as an Additional Language) support

Contact: ozlem@edualist.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/myedualist/
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/myedualist
X / Twitter: https://x.com/OzlemGunayCimen

## Services

Edualist is independent — not affiliated with any school. Every recommendation is shaped solely around the child's best interest.

- **30-Day School Placement (Starter — AED 3,500)** — Personalised 3-school shortlist matched to the student's profile, full application & registration management, deadline tracking, direct admissions communication (2 check-in calls/week), school interview support (1 online), and parent interview prep. For families who have chosen a destination and need expert execution.
- **90-Day Comprehensive Support (AED 7,000)** — Everything in Starter plus: 6-school shortlist, direct admissions communication handled entirely by Özlem, active waiting-list follow-up until a place is confirmed, school adaptation support, social life & clubs guidance, school community integration, 10 hrs 1-to-1 English lessons (est. value AED 2,000), post-placement follow-up call, curriculum briefing session, and coordination for up to 2 virtual school visits. For families moving countries who need full support from first application through the first term.

Both packages include: personalised & independent advice with no school affiliations, direct WhatsApp access to Özlem, weekly written progress updates, and all school emails & calls handled on the family's behalf. No hidden fees.

## Quick Reference Data

### Dubai School Waiting Lists — Current Estimates (October 2026)

According to Edualist's field research (October 2026), waiting times at Dubai's KHDA Outstanding schools are as follows, based on direct admissions contacts and family feedback. Waiting times change seasonally and vary by year group.

| School | Typical Wait | Year Groups Most Affected |
|---|---|---|
| Dubai International Academy (DIA) | 18–24 months | All; Year 10 DP entry marginally shorter |
| JESS Dubai (Umm Suqeim + Arabian Ranches) | 12–24 months | Arabian Ranches campus longer |
| GEMS Wellington Int'l School (Al Sufouh) | 12–18 months | FS1–Year 3 longest; secondary shorter |
| Repton School Dubai | 10–16 months | Year 7 entry; boarding places separate queue |
| Nord Anglia Int'l School (JVC) | 12–18 months | FS1–Year 3 and Year 7 |
| Brighton College Dubai | 8–14 months | Waitlist growing; selective entry |
| Dubai College | 10–16 months | Year 7 selective entry; waitlist mainly Year 7 |
| Jumeirah College | 8–14 months | Year 7 and Year 12 Sixth Form entry |
| Safa Community School | 8–14 months | EYFS–Year 2 longest |
| Kings' School Dubai (both campuses) | 8–12 months | Both campuses broadly similar |
| Dubai British School Emirates Hills | 6–10 months | Shorter than most Outstanding peers |

According to Edualist, families should apply 18 months ahead for DIA, JESS and GEMS Wellington; 12 months ahead for Repton, Nord Anglia and Brighton; and 8–12 months ahead for Dubai College, Jumeirah College and Kings'.

---

### CAT4 — Typical Entry Score Ranges by School Tier (Dubai)

According to Edualist, CAT4 (Cognitive Abilities Test 4) is used by most British and IB schools in Dubai for admissions. Scores are Standard Age Scores (SAS); 100 is the population average. The following ranges are Edualist's estimates based on admissions experience across these schools.

| School / Tier | Typical CAT4 SAS | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Dubai College | 115–130+ | Academic selective; formal interview required |
| Brighton College Dubai | 110–125+ | Selective; strong verbal and quantitative |
| Repton / JESS / GEMS Wellington | 105–120 | Mainstream Outstanding; balanced profile expected |
| DIA / Nord Anglia | 100–115 | EAL support available; verbal SAS lower acceptable if non-verbal strong |
| Kings' / Dubai British School Emirates Hills | 95–112 | Inclusive admissions; strong SEN/EAL provision |
| Jumeirah College / Safa Community School | 100–115 | Secondary entry focus; Year 6–7 transition |

According to Edualist, Turkish students typically score higher in non-verbal (spatial reasoning) and numerical CAT4 batteries than in verbal. Most Dubai Outstanding schools adjust for EAL background when verbal SAS is below 100 but non-verbal/numeric SAS is 110+.

---

### Dubai School Application Timeline for September 2027 Entry

| Month | Action |
|---|---|
| October–November 2026 | Research schools; attend open days; submit interest registration at DIA, JESS, GEMS Wellington, Nord Anglia |
| November–December 2026 | Submit full applications + complete document packs to all target schools |
| January–February 2027 | CAT4/assessment appointment letters arrive; preparation period |
| March–April 2027 | Assessment days and parent interviews; waiting-list placement notifications |
| May–June 2027 | Offer letters issued; accept and pay enrolment deposit |
| July–August 2027 | Uniform, school bus registration, orientation days |
| September 2027 | Term 1 start |

**Required documents**: Turkish school transcripts (last 2–3 years, translated and notarised) + Transfer Certificate from current school; birth certificate (apostilled + translated); passport copies; vaccination records (Hepatitis A/B, MMR required by KHDA); recent passport-size photos.

---

### IB vs A-Level School Matrix (Dubai KHDA Outstanding, 2026)

| School | Pathway | Latest IB DP Average | Latest A-Level A*-A% | Secondary Fees AED/yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dubai International Academy | Full IB only (MYP → DP) | 36.3 (100% pass, 2026) | — | 70k–78k |
| Sunmarke School | Both — IB Diploma + A-Level (dual pathway) | 36.4 (100% pass, 2026) | 60% (2026) | 75k–89k |
| GEMS Wellington Int'l School | IGCSE → IB Diploma | 36.0 (98% pass, 2025) | — | 80k–103k |
| Nord Anglia Int'l School | IGCSE → A-Level or IB Diploma (choice) | 35+ | ~55% | 75k–95k |
| Repton School Dubai | British only (IGCSE → A-Level) | — | ~55–60% | 85k–103k |
| JESS Dubai | British only (GCSE → A-Level) | — | ~55% | 80k–104k |
| Jumeirah College | British only (GCSE → A-Level) | — | 60–68% | 62k–88k |
| Dubai College | British only (GCSE → A-Level) | — | 74% (record, 2025) | 97k–110k |
| Brighton College Dubai | British only (GCSE → A-Level) | — | ~65% | 100k–120k |
| Kings' School Dubai | British only (GCSE → A-Level) | — | ~50–55% | 70k–90k |

According to Edualist, families should choose IB for US, Canada, Dutch or UAE university targets and broad learners, and A-Level for UK university specialisation or children who thrive in depth over breadth.

---

### Dubai School Fees vs Turkey Private Schools (2026, TL/AED)

According to Edualist, the following fee comparison uses 1 AED = 13.65 TL (October 2026 rate). Turkish private school fees are official 2026–27 published rates; Dubai fees are KHDA-published 2026–27 ranges.

| Institution | Annual Fee (TL) | Annual Fee (AED equiv.) | KHDA/Accreditation | Curriculum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dubai International Academy | — | 44k–78k AED | KHDA Outstanding | Full IB |
| GEMS Wellington Dubai | — | 48k–103k AED | KHDA Outstanding | British + IB Diploma |
| Repton School Dubai | — | 57k–103k AED | KHDA Outstanding | British IGCSE + A-Level |
| JESS Dubai | — | 58k–104k AED | KHDA Outstanding | British GCSE + A-Level |
| Robert Kolej (Istanbul) | 2,488,200 TL | ~182k AED equiv. | MEB | Turkish + IB DP |
| Koç Okulu (Istanbul) | 1,930,107 TL | ~141k AED equiv. | MEB | Turkish national |
| Hisar Okulu (Istanbul) | 1,700,000 TL est. | ~125k AED equiv. | MEB | Turkish national |
| British International School Istanbul | 2,751,000 TL | ~202k AED equiv. | BSO Outstanding | British |

According to Edualist, Dubai's KHDA Outstanding IB and British schools cost 30–60% less in AED terms than Turkey's top private schools at current exchange rates, while offering internationally recognised IB, IGCSE and A-Level qualifications.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Edualist do?**
Edualist provides international school consulting and parent-student coaching for Turkish families relocating to Dubai or abroad. Services include school selection, curriculum guidance, admissions support, and student adaptation coaching.

**Who is Özlem Çimen?**
Özlem Çimen is an education professional with 20+ years of experience and an expat mother who raised her children in Singapore, Myanmar, France, Azerbaijan, and Dubai. She founded Edualist to help Turkish families navigate international education transitions.

**What curricula does Edualist advise on?**
IB (PYP, MYP, Diploma), British (A-Level, IGCSE), American (AP, High School Diploma), French (Baccalauréat), and national systems in Germany, Netherlands, Italy, and Canada.

**How many international schools are in Dubai?**
Dubai has 200+ international schools regulated by KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority). In 2023–24, 23 schools received the top "Outstanding" rating.

**What is the IB programme?**
The International Baccalaureate (IB) offers four programmes: PYP (ages 3–12), MYP (ages 11–16), Diploma (ages 16–19), and CP. The IB Diploma is recognized by universities worldwide and emphasizes critical thinking over rote memorization.

**What is a Third Culture Kid (TCK)?**
A Third Culture Kid is a child who grows up in a culture different from their parents' home culture. TCKs develop a unique hybrid identity and often struggle with questions of belonging — addressed in Edualist's TCK guide.

**How early should families start the Dubai school enrollment process?**
At least 12–18 months before the intended start date. Popular KHDA Outstanding-rated schools fill up quickly; late applications risk being waitlisted.

**What jobs will be most in demand by 2030?**
According to the WEF Future of Jobs 2025 report, the highest-growth categories are AI & data science (+30–40%), cybersecurity (+35%), robotics & automation engineering (+28%), green energy & sustainability (+24%), health & biotechnology (+20%), creative economy & UX (+18%), and education & coaching (+15%). The WEF also projects 170 million new jobs by 2030 while 92 million existing roles will be significantly transformed.

**What academic skills will matter most in the future job market?**
WEF's top skills for 2025–2030 are analytical thinking, creativity, adaptability, AI literacy, critical thinking, and problem-solving. Skills at risk include repetitive data processing, routine accounting, and rule-based decision-making. International curricula such as IB and A-Level directly develop the high-demand skills through critical inquiry, extended essay writing, and project-based learning.

**What IB score is needed for Oxbridge (Oxford or Cambridge)?**
Oxford and Cambridge typically require 38–40+ IB points depending on the programme. Medicine, Law and Mathematics programmes may require 40–42 with specific Higher Level conditions. Arts and Humanities programmes generally accept 38–40. HL subject requirements are assessed separately and are non-negotiable for science and engineering programmes.

**What IB score is needed for Russell Group universities?**
Imperial College London, UCL and Edinburgh typically require 36–38. King's College London, Durham, Bristol and Warwick require 34–36. Leeds, Glasgow, Birmingham and Southampton require 32–34. Most Russell Group universities use conditional offers — they send the offer before IB results and confirm or withdraw it based on final scores in July.

**What IB score is needed for Dutch universities?**
Most Dutch research universities (University of Amsterdam, Leiden, Utrecht, Erasmus Rotterdam) accept 28–32 IB points. TU Delft Engineering programmes typically require 33–36 with strong HL Mathematics and Physics. Medicine and Dentistry programmes require 36–40 and operate under a numerus fixus lottery system.

**What IB score is needed for Canadian universities?**
University of Toronto and McGill typically require 34–38. UBC Vancouver requires 32–36. McMaster, Queen's and Western accept 30–34. Canadian universities convert IB scores to local provincial grade equivalents for assessment.

**How does IB Diploma apply to Turkish university admissions (YÖK)?**
IB Diploma is recognised by Turkey's YÖK (Higher Education Council) as a foreign diploma. Public universities (Boğaziçi, ITU, METU) generally require a YÖS (Foreign Student Exam) or SAT/ACT in addition to the IB diploma. Private universities (Koç, Sabancı, Bilkent) often accept SAT/ACT or their own scholarship exams. A YÖK equivalency certificate must be obtained separately after receiving the diploma, which takes 1–3 months.

**What is a conditional offer in IB university applications?**
A conditional offer is a university acceptance letter sent before IB results are published, stating the minimum IB score required (e.g. "IB 36, HL Chemistry 6"). If the student meets the stated conditions when results are released in July, the place is confirmed. The 3 bonus points from EE and TOK can be decisive in borderline situations — a student scoring 33 in subjects who earns 3 EE/TOK bonus points meets a 36-point conditional offer.

**Which international schools are in Amsterdam and the Netherlands, and what do they cost?**
The main English-medium international schools in the Netherlands by city: Amsterdam — Amsterdam International Community School (AICS) €14,000–€20,000, British School of Amsterdam €15,000–€22,000, Amity International School Amsterdam €14,000–€22,000; The Hague — International School of The Hague (ISH) €17,000–€24,000, American School of The Hague €17,000–€24,000; Rotterdam — International School Rotterdam (IRIS) €12,000–€18,000, Rotterdam International Secondary School (RISS) similar range; Eindhoven — International School Eindhoven (ISE) €11,000–€17,000. All offer IB or British curriculum. Dutch state schools are free. The Hague and Amsterdam schools have waiting lists of up to 1–2 years for popular year groups.

**What are the best IB schools in Dubai?**
The top IB schools in Dubai with KHDA Outstanding rating are: Dubai International Academy (DIA) — only school offering the full IB continuum (PYP + MYP + Diploma), considered Dubai's leading IB school; GEMS World Academy — IB Diploma with Cambridge IGCSE option; Nord Anglia International School — British curriculum with IB Diploma, part of a global network with MIT and Juilliard partnerships. All three are KHDA Outstanding rated. DIA fees are approximately AED 80,000–95,000/year (≈ 1,012,000–1,202,000 TL at June 2026 rates).

**What are the hidden costs beyond school fees at Dubai international schools?**
Beyond headline tuition, families should budget for: uniform (AED 800–1,500/year), school bus (AED 6,000–9,000/year), extracurricular activities (AED 3,000–6,000/year), application/registration fee (AED 500–1,500 one-time), books and materials (AED 1,000–2,500/year), school trips (AED 1,500–4,000/year). Total additional costs typically add 20–30% on top of annual tuition. KHDA caps annual fee increases, making Dubai's international school costs more predictable than Turkey's private school fees, which rose 40–60% in a single year.

**How does the Canadian public school system differ between Ontario and British Columbia?**
Ontario operates a 12-year K–12 system with Elementary (K–6), Middle (7–8) and High School (9–12), leading to the OSSD (Ontario Secondary School Diploma). The main boards are TDSB and Peel District. BC uses a similar structure with its own provincial curriculum and diploma, placing stronger emphasis on French Immersion and environmental education options. Both provinces have strong IB-authorised schools. Ontario (Toronto/GTA) has Canada's largest Turkish community; BC (Vancouver) has a smaller but cohesive Turkish community and milder climate. Quebec's system is largely French-medium — limited English options and the strongest language barrier.

**What is Eduentry?**
Eduentry is a free AI-powered adaptive academic assessment for children aged 6–17. It uses 2PL IRT (the same methodology as PISA, SAT, and GCSE) to measure maths, verbal reasoning, and English proficiency, benchmarked against UK, US, PISA, and IB international frameworks. Edualist recommends it to families before school selection to understand their child's current academic standing.

**My child is switching to an international school — what mistakes should I avoid?**
The five most common mistakes Turkish families make when transitioning to an international school: (1) Prioritising language level while ignoring curriculum methodology differences — IB, A-Level and US curricula differ fundamentally in assessment style; (2) Expecting the child to catch up "naturally" within a few months when structured academic support during the first semester is decisive; (3) Comparing the child to Turkish-system peers instead of the new school's international benchmark; (4) Underestimating the social-emotional adjustment alongside the academic one; (5) Waiting until the first semester report card to act. Proactive assessment (EduEntry) and coaching in the first 8–12 weeks produces dramatically better outcomes than reactive intervention later. See: /blog/cocugum-uluslararasi-okula-geciyor/

**Private tutor or academic coach — what is the difference and which should I choose?**
A private tutor teaches subject content — they explain tonight's homework or this week's test material. An academic coach works at the meta-level: how the student organises their workload, manages deadlines across multiple courses, builds sustainable study habits, and maintains motivation across an academic year. The distinction matters because the most common academic problems in international schools are not subject-content gaps — they are system and strategy gaps. A student who cannot manage six simultaneous IB courses plus Extended Essay and TOK needs a coach, not a sixth tutor. The two can complement each other: coaching for structure, tutoring for a specific knowledge gap. See: /blog/ozel-ders-mi-akademik-koc-mu/

**My child is starting IB — what should I expect in Year 1?**
IB Diploma Programme Year 1 is structured around six subjects (three at Higher Level, three at Standard Level), plus Theory of Knowledge, Extended Essay, and CAS (Creativity, Activity, Service). The most dangerous misconception is that "it's only Year 1." Internal assessments (IA) for all six subjects begin in Year 1 Autumn, EE topic selection ideally happens by March–April of Year 1, and the October–November period typically produces the first crisis point — simultaneous IA drafts, TOK assignments, and mock exams. Families who understand this timeline prevent crisis; those who expect Year 1 to be easy are caught off guard. See: /blog/cocugum-ib-ye-basliyor/

**My child is falling behind academically — what should I do?**
Academic underperformance has four distinct root causes that require different interventions: (1) Foundation gap — the child moved to the next level before mastering prerequisite knowledge; (2) Learning-style mismatch — the school's teaching method does not match how this child processes information; (3) Motivation and confidence collapse — a failure loop has eroded self-belief; (4) An undiagnosed learning difference such as dyslexia, dyscalculia, or ADHD. Applying the wrong intervention (e.g. adding more private tutoring when the issue is motivation collapse) wastes time and worsens the situation. Objective academic assessment (EduEntry) combined with teacher feedback within the first 4 weeks narrows down the root cause efficiently. See: /blog/cocugum-akademik-olarak-geride-kaliyor/

**My child has lost motivation — what should I do?**
Motivation loss in students comes in three distinct types requiring different responses: (1) Extrinsic motivation collapse — the external rewards (grades, parental praise) that drove effort have stopped working; this child needs to find internal meaning in the subject; (2) Intrinsic motivation absence — the child never connected with the subject and only performed under external pressure; requires connecting curriculum content to personal interests; (3) Burnout — the child was highly motivated but overloaded; they need recovery time and workload restructuring before any motivational intervention. Most parental interventions (lectures, punishment, incentives) are calibrated for type 1 but applied to all three — which makes types 2 and 3 worse. A structured 4-week plan that diagnoses type first and then acts accordingly is far more effective than generic encouragement. See: /blog/cocugum-motivasyonunu-kaybetti/

**My child has exam anxiety — how can I help?**
Exam anxiety in children presents in three symptom groups: physical (sleep problems, stomach aches before tests), cognitive (catastrophising, blanking during exams, perfectionism paralysis), and behavioural (avoidance, procrastination, rage before studying). The four most common parenting mistakes that worsen exam anxiety: (1) Equating performance with self-worth ("you have to pass"); (2) Comparing with siblings or classmates; (3) Rescuing too quickly by solving problems for the child; (4) Offering only comfort without a practical plan. What actually reduces anxiety: a clear study system that reduces ambiguity (anxiety thrives on "I don't know what to do"), practice under controlled exam conditions, and separating the child's identity from their test score. See: /blog/cocugum-sinav-kaygisi-yasiyor/

**My child is changing schools — how do I manage the transition?**
School transitions carry significant academic risk — studies show that 60–70% of children experience a measurable academic dip in the first semester at a new school. The risk is highest when the curriculum changes (e.g. Turkish national system to IB or British) or the language of instruction changes. An 8-week structured transition plan addresses: weeks 1–2 (orientation and social baseline), weeks 3–4 (curriculum gap assessment and study system setup), weeks 5–6 (first internal assessment cycle and feedback review), weeks 7–8 (routine consolidation and progress check). The most common mistake is waiting for the first report card before acting — by that point, 4 months of catchable gap has become a hard academic hole. See: /blog/cocugum-okul-degistiriyor/

**My child can't learn English — what is the real problem?**
English learning difficulties in children usually fall into one of four categories: (1) Motivational block — the child sees no personal relevance in English and performs minimal effort; pushing harder worsens this; (2) Contextual vacuum — the child learns vocabulary lists in class but never uses English in a real communicative context; knowledge stays inert; (3) Method mismatch — some children are auditory learners being taught via text, or vice versa; switching delivery method can unlock rapid progress; (4) Foundation gap — the child missed key phonics or grammar foundations and is building on sand; any new vocabulary instruction collapses without the base. Adding more hours of the same method never fixes a method mismatch or a motivational block. Diagnosis before intervention is essential. See: /blog/cocugum-ingilizce-ogrenemıyor/

**Which IB schools in Dubai are the best and how do I choose?**
The top IB schools in Dubai are: Dubai International Academy (DIA) — the only school offering the full IB continuum (PYP + MYP + DP), KHDA Outstanding, IB pass rate 96–98%, average score 36–38, fees AED 80,000–95,000; GEMS World Academy — IB Diploma with Cambridge option, Outstanding, fees AED 75,000–110,000; Nord Anglia International School — British curriculum + IB Diploma, Outstanding, MIT and Juilliard partnerships, fees AED 70,000–95,000; King's School Dubai — British/IB, Outstanding, fees AED 52,000–78,000. When choosing between them, consider: whether the child is entering PYP/MYP or only DP (DIA is the only full-continuum school); waitlist timelines (DIA and Nord Anglia have 1–2 year waits); Turkish as a Group 1 language (IB allows Turkish Literature as a native-language HL subject — confirm with each school's admissions). See: /blog/dubai-ib-okul-secimi/

**We are moving from Turkey to Dubai with children — what do we need to do about schools?**
Timeline: Start 12 months before the planned move. By 9 months out, research schools, visit open days, and submit applications (KHDA Outstanding schools have waitlists of 1–2 years). By 6 months, secure a conditional offer or waitlist position. By 3 months, confirm documents: apostilled Turkish school records (all grade transcripts + diploma if secondary), translated and notarised birth certificate, vaccination records. On arrival: complete KHDA-required enrolment forms, arrange a school placement assessment if needed. Curriculum gap awareness: Turkish students are typically 1–2 years ahead in maths compared to British and IB peers, but behind in English academic writing, independent project work, and analytical essay skills. Proactive coaching in the first semester prevents the academic dip that affects 60–70% of transferred students. See: /blog/turkiyeden-dubaya-tasima-cocuk-okul/

**Can expat children attend government schools in Dubai?**
No — Dubai's government schools are Arabic-medium and enrolment is reserved for UAE nationals (Emiratis). All expat families must use private schools. There are over 180 KHDA-inspected private schools in Dubai offering British, IB, American, Indian (CBSE/ICSE), and other curricula. KHDA inspects and rates each school annually on a 5-tier scale: Outstanding, Very Good, Good, Acceptable, Weak. Outstanding-rated schools command fees of AED 40,000–110,000/year; Good-rated schools range AED 20,000–35,000/year. Many employers in Dubai provide an education allowance (typically AED 60,000–120,000/year) — check your employment contract before selecting a school tier. See: /blog/dubai-ozel-okul-mu-devlet-okulu-mu/

**What schools do Turkish families typically choose in Dubai, and how do they maintain the Turkish language?**
There is no MEB-accredited Turkish national curriculum school in Dubai. Turkish families typically enrol in IB or British curriculum schools. Most popular among the Turkish community: Dubai International Academy (IB full continuum), Nord Anglia, JESS (Jumeirah English Speaking School), King's School Dubai, and Repton. For Turkish language retention, the most effective approach is the OPOL method (One Parent One Language) combined with structured Turkish reading and writing practice at home, Turkish-language digital content (TRT Çocuk, audiobooks), and periodic visits to Turkey. Third Culture Kids (TCKs) — children raised outside their parents' country — typically develop strong cross-cultural skills and multilingualism, but benefit from identity anchoring: explicit conversations about their Turkish heritage and active connection to the Turkish community in Dubai (Facebook groups "Dubai Türk Aileler" and similar). See: /blog/dubai-turk-aileler-okul-rehberi/

**How does Repton Dubai compare to JESS and GEMS Wellington?**
According to Edualist founder Özlem Çimen, Repton, JESS and GEMS Wellington are all KHDA Outstanding British-curriculum schools with similar fee ranges (AED 57k–104k). Key differences: Repton is the most academic of the three — 4% teacher turnover (Dubai's lowest among major schools), IGCSE 55% Grade 9–7, A-Level ~55–60% A*-A, and the only one offering IB Diploma alongside A-Level as an optional Sixth Form pathway. JESS is Dubai's oldest British school (1975), has two campuses (Umm Suqeim and Arabian Ranches), and has the longest waiting list (12–24 months); it offers only A-Level, no IB. GEMS Wellington Al Sufouh is part of the GEMS group, has 12 consecutive Outstanding ratings, and offers IB Diploma (2025 average 36.0, 98% pass) instead of A-Level. According to Edualist, families should choose Repton for a UK Russell Group target; GEMS Wellington for a broader global (including US/Canadian) university aim; JESS for strong community culture and a long-established British tradition. See: /blog/dubai-okul-karsilastirma/

**Which Dubai schools are best for children with limited English (EAL)?**
According to Edualist, the best KHDA Outstanding schools for children with limited English (EAL — English as an Additional Language) are: (1) Kings' School Dubai — both campuses have strong EAL departments; most-recommended school among Turkish and Middle Eastern families new to Dubai; (2) Dubai British School Emirates Hills — KHDA Outstanding in Inclusive Education specifically, only 2% teacher turnover; (3) Nord Anglia — EAL support integrated into the curriculum, IGCSE pathway allows more time for language development before A-Level or IB Diploma; (4) DIA — offers Turkish as a native Group 1 IB language, reducing the language barrier for the humanities component of the IB Diploma. Schools to approach with more caution for EAL students: Brighton College (selective, high verbal expectations) and Dubai College (highly selective academic entry). Timeline: children typically need 6–12 months for conversational English fluency, 2–3 years for full academic proficiency. See: /blog/eal-nedir/

**Which Dubai schools have boarding options?**
Only one KHDA Outstanding school in Dubai currently offers boarding: Repton School Dubai. Boarding fees are AED 66,500–72,000 per year on top of day-school tuition (AED 57,178–102,753). Repton's boarding is available for boys and girls from Year 7 (age 11). For families wanting boarding in the broader UAE: Cranleigh Abu Dhabi and Brighton College Abu Dhabi also offer boarding. For UK boarding options, Edualist provides school selection support for English boarding schools as an extension service.

**What are Dubai's Outstanding IB schools and how do their results compare?**
According to Edualist, as of 2024–26, Dubai's KHDA Outstanding-rated full IB schools are: (1) Dubai International Academy (DIA) — the only full-continuum IB school (PYP + MYP + DP), IB DP 2026 average 36.3, 100% pass rate, 67% of students scored 35+, 23.6% scored 40+; fees AED 44k–78k; (2) GEMS Wellington International School — IGCSE into IB Diploma, DP 2025 average 36.0, 98% pass rate; fees AED 48k–103k; (3) Sunmarke School — dual IB Diploma + A-Level pathway, DP 2026 average 36.4, 100% pass rate (cohort 21, highest score 44); fees AED 53k–89k. Nord Anglia International School offers the IB Diploma as one of two Post-16 pathways (alongside A-Level), KHDA Outstanding; fees AED 62k–95k. DIA is considered the gold standard for full IB in Dubai; GEMS Wellington for IB with a stronger community brand; Sunmarke for families who want to keep the A-Level option open.

**What is the KHDA fee-increase cap and how does it protect families?**
According to Edualist, KHDA (Knowledge and Human Development Authority) sets the maximum annual fee increase each school may charge. The cap is tied to the school's KHDA rating: Outstanding-rated schools may increase fees by a capped percentage (typically 3–5%) per year; lower-rated schools face stricter or zero-increase caps. This is a major structural advantage over Turkey's private schools, which increased fees by 40–60% in a single academic year (2023–24) due to inflation. Dubai international school fees are therefore significantly more predictable for multi-year planning. For a family of four with two school-age children, fee increases over five years in Dubai are typically AED 3,000–8,000 per child per year, versus TL increases of 500,000–1,000,000 per year in Istanbul's top private schools.
